speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. As the Prime Minister will know, yesterday counsel for the government tried to withhold from the McDonald royal commission certain government documents. The Prime Minister will also recall that on October 25 of this year he said, as reported at page 450 of Hansard:
-we would produce and have produced every document asked for.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister, is that still the position of the government, and will the government instruct its counsel to make available to the McDonald royal commission all government documents, all documents in the possession of the government, relevant to the inquiry of the McDonald commission.
October 27, 1978

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I am informed, what happened yesterday before the commission is that counsel for former commissioner Higgitt asked for the production of documents without any notice either to the government or to the commission itself. Naturally, both the commission and ourselves think that this is a procedure which should be corrected.
I repeat my assurance that we will co-operate by making all documents available to the commission. We will, further, co-operate in making public any documents which the commission wants to make public and which are any evidence of wrongdoing. But in order to co-operate, we have to know what is asked for and we must have notice of what documents are to be produced, so that we can consider their classification and consider their declassification if the commission so requires.
It was just a matter of the government and the commission having been caught by surprise with documents that they did not know were going to be asked for. I think that it proves once again the unfairness, in terms of due process of law, of proceeding in this way in public without complete co-operation on the procedures to be followed.

subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that it was simply by inadvertence, but I think the Prime Minister declined or neglected to answer my question as to whether or not there will be an instruction to counsel to make available the particular documents in question. I would like him to clarify that, and elaborate on the significance of the phrase he used when he said that the government would want to consider the classification of the documents that would be made available to the McDonald royal commission.
Does that mean there are, in the possession of the government, government documents which have a classification that in the view of the government makes it improper or impossible for the government to make those documents available to the McDonald royal commission? In other words, are there some documents that this government will not make available to the McDonald royal commission?

subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly not documents that it would be improper to show to them. As I said the other day, the government does not attempt to absolve itself of its responsibility for the protection of secret documents and Privy Council secrets. I have said that when the commission feels that such documents which are covered by the necessities of secrecy should be published, and that they show evidence of some wrongdoing, we will undertake to declassify them.
I cannot say in advance that we will declassify all documents in every circumstance and permit them to be made public. We will do so when they show evidence of wrongdoing, in the judgment of the commission, and when in the judgment of the commission it is important to make these documents public. The Leader of the Opposition will realize that probably even the McDonald commission will not want to make all docu-
Oral Questions
ments public, any more than any other royal commission of inquiry into matters of secrecy and intelligence.

subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is perhaps confusion here between the question of the production of documents and the question of publication of documents. I want to come to the question of publication later. I want to be absolutely clear, here, on the question of production of documents.
Is it the position of the government that the government will make available to the McDonald royal commission every single document, regardless of classification, which might in any way be relevant to the inquiry of the McDonald commission? I am not speaking here of publication-that is another question-I am speaking of production. Is there going to be any limitation at all upon the documents that the Government of Canada will make available to this commission?

subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am informed that the commission has had access to all these documents. Therefore, it is not a question of not showing them to the commission. The commission has had access to the RCMP files, and presumably knows about these documents. The debate yesterday was about whether they should be produced at that particular stage.

subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister and I have a slightly different views of what went on yesterday before the commission. For the record, and in very unequivocal terms, I should like to have from the Prime Minister a categorical assurance that every document that is relevant to the McDonald royal commission that is a government document, or is in possession of the government, will be made available to the McDonald royal commission and that no question of classification will stand as a bar to the production by the government of relevant material to that commission.

subsubtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that undertaking can be given in a general way. I cannot say in advance that all cabinet minutes can, or should, be put before the royal commission without the government asking itself if this has to be done. If the royal commission makes a case for access to cabinet committee minutes as is the case with the documents which were asked to be produced yesterday, my answer is yes. I saw the cabinet committee minute just five minutes before I came to the House. Certainly, the government would have no objection to producing that cabinet committee minute.
I do not think the discussion in cabinet of every and all subjects should be available to any outsiders of cabinet. I think this is a clear doctrine of cabinet secrecy, and it will be preserved.

subtopic: INDEMNIFICATION OF COURT COSTS OF MEMBERS OF FORCE
INDEMNIFICATION OF COURT COSTS OF MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to pursue the uncertainty that seems to have been created. I think it is important, in addressing my question through you to the Solicitor General, to clear up something that happened last

October 27, 1978
Oral Questions
Wednesday, when the Solicitor General told me that to the best of his knowledge there was no government policy that would permit the indemnification or protection of RCMP officers who, acting through the tacit or expressed approval of their superiors, might have transgressed the law.
There has now been made public, as the Solicitor General knows, clear and detailed documentary evidence that such a policy existed, at least within the force, as long ago as 1970.
My question to the Solicitor General is, has he conferred with any of his five or four predecessors in office: if it is not within his knowledge, has he conferred with his predecessors to determine whether it was within their knowledge during their respective terms of office? If so, have they confirmed, or denied, knowledge of this policy? If they have confirmed having knowledge, could he tell us when they became aware of that policy of protection and indemnification?

subtopic: INDEMNIFICATION OF COURT COSTS OF MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 stand by what I said on Wednesday, that there is no information that has come to me from either interviews with my predecessors or with officials who have been in place since the early part of the 1970s indicating that there was any knowledge within the government of a policy within the RCMP as described by the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: INDEMNIFICATION OF COURT COSTS OF MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Solicitor General will not tell me if he has consulted with and asked the specific question of his predecessors. I would think it would be incumbent upon him to do so. The Solicitor General is aware, from the documentary evidence, that the protection and indemnification policies resulted from prolonged consultation among the highest-ranking officers in the force, being exactly the same officers who were consulting weekly with this series of solicitors general: the very same officers.
In view of these circumstances, can the Solicitor General offer the House any reasonable explanation whatsoever as to how a policy so important, so fundamental to the operation of the force for which the Solicitor General is responsible, could be in effect as long as eight years without any of this series of solicitors general being aware of it?

subtopic: INDEMNIFICATION OF COURT COSTS OF MEMBERS OF FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman fully recognizes that the matter is one that is presently being studied by the McDonald inquiry in terms of its being internal RCMP policy. That matter, of course, is now subject to direct examination of former commissioner Higgitt and potential cross-examination in the near future.
As I have indicated before, it is not my intention now, relating to matters before the commission, to start commenting on either the direct examination or cross-examination that may be adduced. In terms of what was government policy, my statement is categorical, that to the best of my knowledge there has not been any policy of this government indicating that there was condonation or, indeed, acceptance of illegal activity on the part of the RCMP.

PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister a question relating to his earlier answers. Since the documents in question at the inquiry yesterday were requested to corroborate Mr. Higgitt's allegations or claims that certain ministers of the Crown knew of certain illegal or inappropriate activities, and since government counsel, on instruction from the government, objected to the introduction of these documents not simply at this time but in general, in part on the grounds that some of the documents were not appropriately in the hands of the RCMP in the first place, I ask the Prime Minister if he would reconsider his earlier answer.
Why did the government instruct its counsel to block the presentation of these documents, which could be used in a fair-minded way to either confirm or deny Mr. Higgitt's allegations, for submission either for public assessment or simply for consideration in camera by the commission?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not given any such instruction and I do not know of any such instructions regarding the particular documents produced yesterday. There is a general policy, which I have tried to explain in this House, which applies generally to the government's attitude before the commission.
I cannot comment on the hearing that went on yesterday, because I did not read what they said. As I say, I was informed five minutes before coming into this House about a certain cabinet minute. I was asked if I would permit its declassification and I said, "Sure": if the commission wants to declassify this particular one, I see no reason not to. That will remain my policy and it is the policy of the government.
[DOT] (U27)
Whether the lawyers yesterday were acting on specific instructions in that case, or on my general instructions-ones I have just stated-I do not know. But my information is that it must have been, in this particular case, that they objected because they had not been notified of what documents would be produced. The commission itself was not notified, and it was sprung on the commission.
Once again I appeal to the House and I appeal to the Canadian public to keep the due process of law in mind. One party has a lawyer making some allegations in front of the court. If the opposition is interested in having the truth come out, let us see what the lawyers for the other side will say; let us see what the documents will eventually say, if they are produced; and if they are not produced, let us find out why. But let us not draw the conclusion that the government is trying to hide a document which it did not know would be produced until, apparently, the moment it was produced yesterday. That is all that is being asked for, due process and fairness, and not just jumping to conclusions because a lawyer for one party has suggested that something be adduced in evidence without the other side hearing about it.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, the reasonable note of the Prime Minister's answer does not accord with the facts. Counsel fo* the government said before the commission yesterday-and I quote him as he is quoted in the press-that he was instructed, presumably by the government, presumably by the Minister of Justice or someone representing the government: he is quoted as having said:
I am instructed to tell you that the RCMP is not an authorized possessor of the documents. The government objects to them even being shown to the witness-
I say to the Prime Minister, that is counsel acting on behalf of the government telling the commission that he has been instructed so to act. 1 do not think there is much doubt about that, and I find it a little strange that the Prime Minister would not be briefed on this fundamental matter until five minutes before the question period.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister, in this context, going back to the question of the Leader of the Opposition earlier, whether the Prime Minister is now saying that he will be the final arbiter in deciding which documents are appropriate for the commission to see. subtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know from what report the hon. member is reading. 1 do know, because I was so informed a few minutes ago, that a particular series of documents-four, I believe-were sprung on the commission yesterday and sprung on the government by the lawyer on one side. I am told that the McDonald commission itself expressed annoyance at this way of proceeding, precisely because when something happens in this way, of course, it makes the headlines and raises indignation across the country and from the opposition benches. This is not the way we think things should proceed.
Once again, I do not know from what report the Leader of the NDP is reading, but if my information is correct, that this information was sprung on counsel for the commission and counsel for the government, then obviously there could not be an instruction relating to those documents which had been given to counsel. They had no instructions; they were caught by surprise and they said, "Okay, what other documents do you want? Let us look at them. The government has always co-operated, shown them to the commission and co-operated when necessary and declassified them. Presumably we will do that in the future. But let us know if you want a document to be produced, and let us know if you want us to declassify it, so that then we can get instructions from the government."
This seems a perfectly normal attitude to be taken by counsel for the government, when the government is responsible for protecting the confidentiality of documents.

I say, with respect, that the Prime Minister did not answer the crucial question-the question I put to him two days ago, too-about the government's attitude with regard to allowing the commission to determine what it should see, rather than having the government decide.
Oral Questions
The Prime Minister made the case two days ago in this House-he referred to this question today-that certain conversations or discussions in cabinet are confidential and that he would not, as a principle, reveal such documents to the commission if he thought it was none of their business. But what is at stake here is the credibility and integrity of the government itself.
Would the Prime Minister not agree that it is absolutely essential that the commission should have the right to acquire and have access to any conversations which took place in cabinet which might indicate, for example, that ministers had knowledge of wrongdoing? Would he not agree that ultimately it should be the commission, and not the government, which makes that decision?

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS TO MCDONALD COMMISSION
speechtext:
I repeat, if any document can convey knowledge or implication of wrongdoing by the government, we shall co-operate in any way if the commission wants to make it public. To use the expression used by the Minister of Justice, we shall bend over backwards to declassify those documents. But we shall not let the RCMP, the commission, the opposition or the country, have access to all cabinet minutes. We are not going to open all the cabinet minutes for the commission to look into to find out all the discussions which have gone on in cabinet, with the possibility that they are going to find some illegality. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, confidentiality of discussions in cabinet is the most basic principle of cabinet government. It is also based on common sense, which I understand the new member over there has not yet had time to familiarize himself with.
This is the principle I stand by. Any former prime minister would stand by that principle, and I believe any future prime minister would do so. The only alternative is not to have cabinet minutes. If there is not to be free discussion in cabinet, then there should be either no cabinet or no record of its discussions.

The position of the Tory party is that Ontario is a have-not province and should receive equalization payments. If we leave equalization untouched, that is what would happen.
What we want to do with transfer payments to the provinces is establish special job-creating programs to bring about development in the provinces, rather than supporting provincial bureaucracies. We want to have programs like the two we had this summer under the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc). The concept of equalization held by the Tories is that because the premier of Alberta and the premier of Ontario have jets, the premiers of other provinces should also have private planes. That is their concept of equalization.
We want to use federal spending power to help people find jobs. We want to create jobs and to help in the development of the provinces, and that is what the people want. I am very happy the Leader of the Opposition has brought up the question of equalization. I am still waiting to hear their position on equalization because, like everything else, they try to be on both sides of the fence. According to the Auditor General's reports of last year and this year, there has been waste in the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and if that kind of waste could eventually be eliminated there would be moneys available for Canada's senior citizens.
I also said earlier that I hope all hon. members will approach the question of pensions as if it were a right rather than charity. Too often increases in pensions are viewed by people in public life as gifts to Canada's senior citizens, when in fact they are earned through contributions to this country prior to old age.
As the lunch hour approached I was trying to make the point that as Canada's population ages, in other words, as the dependency factor for those over 65 increases numerically, we must re-examine what we are doing regarding the basis of guaranteed income supplement payments. Old age security eligibility has been changed. There is a residency requirement for those who were under the age of 18 at the time of change. For every year a person between the ages of 18 and 65 lived in Canada, or was abroad in an accepted capacity of foreign endeavour, such as employment with CIDA, to a maximum of 40 years, that person would get the basic old age pension at age 65. There is no argument there. What I was speaking about was this: the gap between what the person who receives

the old age security pension and the maximum guaranteed income supplement and what the person who gets the old age security pension and some supplement but does not get more supplement because of certain earnings, is not wide enough.
I do not want to take away from those who need money under the guaranteed income supplement, but what is happening as we look at Canada's senior citizens is that individuals who have small bank accounts bonds, some holdings, or a small amount of earnings, are penalized. For every dollar of income they lose 50 cents of supplement.
I have been saying to the government for some time that old age pensioners should be able to earn a certain amount before the supplement is affected, because what is happening is that we are developing a philosophy whereby people are not saving for retirement because they feel they will be penalized. It flows from that philosophy that as all of us approach old age, the thought is that government "will take care of us." The reason we have seen an acceleration of this thought process is that senior citizens who have been independent, who built this country and who gathered for themselves a little nest egg for their old age, suddenly feel vulnerable because of inflation. They just cannot keep up. The expenses senior citizens are required to meet are not at all in keeping with the amount of money they have put aside for their old age. Constantly we remove some of the dignity which is rightfully theirs.
Far too often senior citizens have come to my office and said. "I have a little savings, I have helped build the country, and now I am being penalized." I am not saying that this should be open-ended, that they could earn any amount of money and qualify for a supplement. If that were the case, obviously the entire concept of supplement would be defeated. But let us not penalize those frugal Canadians who are now senior citizens and have some small savings. We should not penalize them to the point where incentives are taken away from those who will be senior citizens in the next few years. That brings out another dimension, the concept of guaranteed annual income.
Only a few years ago the concept of guaranteed annual income had much more political acceptability than it does today. An experiment known as MINCOME has been conducted in Manitoba. A guaranteed annual income was put into place in a specific area of that province. The program cost approximately $17 million. It was a co-operative enterprise between the federal government and the former government of Manitoba. The program ended before the provincial election took place. Perhaps the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) could speak more completely on this since the program was put into place in his area.
The people on MINCOME were taking away the incentive of people who were earning a marginal amount of money and, with a little bit of government help, would have been independent. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of this opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-5 to amend the Old Age Security Act.
After the Speech from the Throne, I said I was deeply moved to see our government responding to the needs of the sectors of our population where people most need our help. It is important that our old age policy reflect this intense desire of senior citizens to keep the full status of citizens, to keep being considered as human beings in the fullest acceptation of the words.
Those who have withdrawn from the labour market without benefiting from a policy of economic growth are finding themselves in a very difficult material situation because of the increase in the over-all prosperity and the resulting rise in the standard of living. Consequently, we should try to adjust incomes to the increased prosperity. I congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) for her obvious interest in improving our social laws. We all know how concerned she is for the lot of small earners in Canada and she has once again proven it.
The government is often asked to do something about the deplorable situation in which older people find themselves but today, Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see that the government I represent is going to help senior citizens by proposing amendments to Bill C-5 to extend the allocation for a period of six months after the death of the pensioner and provide an increase of $20 a month for those who receive a supplement to give the surviving spouse a period in which to adjust. That will result in an additional outlay of $89 million for Quebec in 1979 but we should remember that money will be going back into the economy. Mr. Speaker, an old age policy should first reflect a deep concern for the dignity of older people and also help them maintain their personal independence to the fullest extent possible from a physical, mental and social standpoint.
The measures all hon. members of this House are being asked to pass are extremely urgent. When you think, Mr. Speaker, that in 1961 in Canada 1,400,000 senior citizens were left on their own because the members of their families were unable to take them into their home. The same goes for the province of Quebec where in 1961 740,575 older persons, or 53.7 per cent, lived with a member of their family, either spouses or unmarried children. In Canada, 89,028 older persons lived with people who are not related to them. This is due to a number of factors, namely the lack of sufficient financial resources. I believe we are all aware of it and should care more for our senior citizens' plight since there are now a large

number of older people because of a high birth rate in the years prior to 1930.
Mr. Speaker, according to the final report tabled by the Special Committee on Aging in 1966, the elderly population in Canada is rapidly increasing. Based on a 65 arbitrary age, the number of senior citizens was 1.5 million in 1966. It has increased five times since then, which points to a three million figure around the years 1991. Those trends seem economically alarming, and they are matter for concern. Senior citizens are the only ones in the total population not to fully share in the general prosperity, yet they are entitled to more than those who have not contributed as children and teenagers.
The great majority of our senior citizens earned low salaries throughout their lives, they lived through the great depression and its insecure environment, they had little or no leisure, and they now are far from the affluence that would minimize the vital importance of money, because money is a factor in freedom and self-dependency. One of my constituents told me: "I was, I am and I will always be what I have always been". He wants to express his views with all his strength and energy. No doubt we are all aware of the gap in private pensions between men and women. The enormous gap between men and women as concerns pension plans is due partly to the fact that 60 per cent of women workers are employed in support services or in business where the level of unionization is very low.
There is another important factor: many employers have deliberately taken action to exclude women from their pension plans. Some of these actions are very subtle, such as the development of pensions plans restricted to employees whose wages exceed a certain level which very few women can hope to achieve or pension plans restricted to certain categories of employment where there are very few women. Other employers have been brutally frank. In its report on private pension plans in Canada in 1974, Statistics Canada shows that, at that time, 400 pension plans were reserved exclusively for men and provided explicitly that women were not eligible. Of the 400 employers involved, 47 had implemented a separate plan for their female employees, 93 had a plan exclusively for male managers and 270 others were in the transportation or the construction field where very few women are employed.
Another way to restrict female participation is to set different minimum and maximum ages of eligibility for the plans. According to Statistics Canada, in 1974, 1,400 plans had different minimum ages of eligibility for men and women, the usual requirement being 21 for men and 25 for women. Moreover, 1,200 plans provided for different maximum ages, retirement being usually set at 60 for women and at 65 for men. Employment is not a major income source for most senior citizens, but it remains a major element in the life of approximately 10 per cent of women aged between 65 and 70. Some of them are career women, mostly single, who choose to postpone their retirement, but most are women who need the money and must work part-time for very small wages.

I know that the member for Saskatoon-Big-gar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) is very proud, as I am, of the plan.
But what does big, wealthy, Ontario do when it comes to medicare? For a family of four in Ontario, the medicare premium is $456 per year. If it were not for the opposition, the NDP and the Liberal party in Queen's Park, that premium would be higher than $456; it would be over $528 for a family of four. In Ontario the government collects more money from medicare premiums than it does from resource revenues. Even in oil-rich Alberta, with the billions of dollars of oil money that they have, the medicare premium there for a family of four is $196 a year. And to top that off, Alberta has all kinds of special fees and utilization charges that they put on people when they are sick. For example, they still charge $4 a day for each day after 120 days for level three and level four care in nursing homes.
They have the same thing in Manitoba where they just brought in a special deterrent fee of $7.50 a day on extended care patients. They are talking about bringing back medicare premiums in that province. All of this is because the party in power is of the belief that people should pay as they go, that government is too big and that we have to cut back.
This is something that cannot be overlooked in a debate like this because, if you are going to cut back on government spending, it is not the grants to big companies, the tax breaks to companies like Imperial Oil and so on, that are cut back; it is the money which goes out to the small people such as the old age pensioners.
As a wise old man in my riding once said during an election campaign, "The Liberal party may cut your throat, but the Conservative party will cut it deeper." I think that he is right when it comes to the social plans of the party.
I would like the Conservatives to get up in this House and to tell me exactly where they stand with regard to old age pensions, where they stand when it comes to cost sharing programs with provincial governments, to upgrade the care and incomes of the ordinary people, when it comes to medicare, hospitalization, unemployment insurance, and family allowances. I think that they have had it both ways for too long. That party has been asking for all kinds of cutbacks, but suddenly when people in the arts appeared on Parliament Hill yesterday, there was a Conservative spokesman saying to them, "God, this government has cut back too far," and that was the member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald). When it comes to agriculture, they always have my friend, the member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), sympathizing with farmers and saying, "Well, I don't understand why they cut back by 8 per cent, and cut back on some of these terrific programs." When it comes to social programs such as unemployment insurance, we always have one of the two Bobbsey Twins from Newfoundland, namely, the member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), getting up and saying, "My gosh, they have cut back too far; they are going to hurt people down in Newfoundland." When it comes to the public servants where they want to cut back drastically, they have the newly elected member for Ottawa
October 27, 1978

Centre (Mr. de Cotret) saying, "Oh, no, I'll make representations to them; I'll make sure that they don't cut back."
One of the issues in a debate like this when we are talking about increases in the old age pensions is whether or not the members of this House are really committed to helping the old people. As the member for Winnipeg North Centre said, a $20 increase is a good increase, but it does not go far enough. We must keep the pressure on the treasury benches to increase the old age pension for those who need it.
Every time I go out among the old people in this country I find that a lot of them are living on the poverty line, not getting enough money to buy the nutritious foods they need, and in big cities particularly a lot of them cannot afford decent housing. It should not be forgotten that these are the people who built this country, the people whose sweat, toil and blood made Canada what it is. I think we owe them more than a small pittance in their old age pension cheque.
The second point I want to make is that we agree with the increase in the old age supplement and with the extension of six months for the spouse's allowance when the elder spouse dies. These are good measures. The spouse's allowance did not exist until a few years ago and, while it helps a lot of people, it still discriminates against single people between ages 60 and 65 who cannot work, and against spinsters, widows, and others. When I go knocking at doors in my riding, many people will say to me, "My neighbour can get the spouse's allowance-in other words, a pension; why can't I get it?"
Even if we pass this bill today, what happens to the spouses who were there yesterday and whose husband or wife passed away? And what happens when the six months are up? The old man is still dead. In 98 per cent of cases the survivor is the wife. She gets an extra six months of grace, but what happens then? Is she to go to the welfare office? The spouse's allowance has created a lot hardships, Mr. Speaker.
I know of a case in the city of Melville where the husband was ten years older than the wife. He had been a small farmer who retired to the city and bought a small house with the proceeds of his farm. All of a sudden he died of a heart attack, although he had not been sick a day in his life. His wife had turned 60 and had qualified for the spouse's allowance. She called my office to know what to do, and it was one of the saddest things I have ever witnessed to see her cry. She had lost her pension, her spouse's allowance, and she did not have any savings. All the money from the farm had gone to buy the house in the city. She was too proud to ask for welfare, but at age 60 she had no training or skills to offer. All her life her work had been on the farm and raising a family. I had to advise her to do the only thing possible and apply for social assistance. That is not easy for someone with the tremendous pride she had in the work she had put into our country and into raising a family. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says it happens to some 200 women every month, and I am sure the story I have told could be repeated by every member of the House.

I know if the Minister of National Health and Welfare were the minister of finance-and according to yesterday's Hansard, I know she wants to be-she would not be the scrooge the present minister is. We would not then have such discrimination against these old people.
My friend from New Brunswick says the minister is not a villain. I would be interested in knowing who the villain is. Is it the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce? I know he changed horses, but he is still riding the same old nag. If it is not the Minister of Finance, I would be interested to know who the scrooge is across the way.
Our party has said for years that the old age pension age should be brought down progressively from 65 to 60 for those people no longer in the labour market. If that were done we would not be discriminating against people on the spouse's allowance who have lost their partners, and we would not discriminate against single people between ages 60 and 65, people who have been widowed and people in that general age group who need help through no fault of their own. I know that many people say that it is too much, that government has grown too big, that government cannot afford that. Still, we can afford that kind of money for empty buildings, and the kind of money for cabinet ministers to fly around in executive aircraft. We can provide that kind of money for tax concessions for big companies, so why is there not enough for the old people between ages 60 and 65 to provide them with their daily bread? The people who would get this money would spend it on consumer items and thus stimulate the economy and provide the jobs that are needed.
I know the Minister of National Health and Welfare is going in the face of many people on the rather conservative side of our society who say that pensions are too big, that indexing should not continue, and that the money should be spent in other places. I happen to disagree with that. I think we need a real stimulus for the economy, and the way to do this is to work from the bottom and put the spending power in the hands of the little people. They spend money on things like shoes, shelter, food, things that stimulate the economy and provide the badly needed jobs.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I should like to encourage the House to pass this bill and regard it as another step toward making life more decent and humane for our older people. They are the real pioneers of Canada; they wanted a country that was strong, that was united, that had equality between people and between regions.

Some times I get some of the old Hansard and read some of her speeches although I regret I do not have more time for this. I say jokingly to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that he has given that kind of speech so many times that I sometimes wondered if he was not using some of her earlier speeches as a text. It indicates how slow social progress really is. It indicates why it needs so many people to be committed to it to keep making demands, because many of the issues the hon. member talked about many years ago in this House are the kinds of legislative action we are taking at this time.
I would also like to join with my colleague, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), in saying to the official opposition that I think this is a moment of truth for them. Many speakers have commented on exactly where they stand respecting some of the social issues, preaching for government restraint and a cutback in programs. But the minute that there is a change they go out and champion everyone who is affected by it. I think this just brings out the tremendous division in their party, between members who come from slower growth areas who are supportive of this kind of legislation, and those who for political reasons, say a very different thing.
The position that members have been taking in the House on some of this legislation has been stated, but I would raise the point of what I think is more serious, and that is what some of them say outside the House. The difficulties that we have in advancing social legislation as a result of some of the very, in my opinion, deplorable positions that certain of them have taken, in terms of trying to convince Canadian people that governments are too socialistic or that we have destroyed the work ethic, and the kind of social objectives I am sure all

members on this side support, are not in the best interests of the country.
Last night when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was speaking, he mentioned that he well remembers living through some of the depression years and how elderly people were looked after during that period of time. I am not nearly as old as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but having been raised in rural Ontario it is not impossible for me to think back to the days when elderly people had a most difficult time. In the neighbourhood where I came from, people by today's standards would be long retired and would be receiving not only old age assistance but also the supplement. Presumably they would be living at a reasonable standard. However, not that many years ago these people were almost totally dependent on the generosity of their families, and lived in accommodation that was not the best. They had very limited opportunity to travel to occupy their minds, and at such time as the farm or other enterprise was taken over, their only occupation was to sort of vegetate. I think Canada has come a long way since then in terms of social legislation.
I am glad to see that we are moving on this bill. It seems to me the present generation of senior citizens deserve support and help almost more than any other generation. If one recalls, senior citizens of today lived through the depression. They were the ones who gave up a lot of economic opportunity to help the war effort, and they have not had available to them any of the programs that people who are middle aged or younger have had. They may not have had the opportunity to prepare for their older years as much as some of us have had.
1 am also pleased that we are dealing with this bill at the present time because it gives us an opportunity to show that we do stand for this. I have been concerned, along with other members who have spoken earlier, about the attack on pensions, and the indexing provision in pensions. It is always interesting to note that the people who attack these things, generally speaking are well off and have very little to fear if there is any change in the indexing procedure or any change in the level of pensions. It is good to see that the government is committed to do that, and to increase further those rights.
I want to state, as other members have, that the next move will need to be to look at the spouse's allowance. It seems to me there is agreement on all sides of the House, at least from the speeches I have heard so far on this bill, C-5, that there would be little trouble in advancing that. I think I am correct if I say the cost of providing the spouse's allowance for those people between the ages of 60 and 65 who would qualify would be in the order of $600 million a year, which is some considerable amount. I would hope that in terms of reviewing government expenditures and the validity of government programs etc., before too long the money could be found, money that is being spent in other areas, and redirected to this area. In my opinion, it is a just and necessary social aspect on which we should move.
My purpose in rising was to make one point, and I would like to do that now. Perhaps I could suggest to the minister than when continuing to review the problem of the spouse's
October 27, 1978

allowance some thought be given to a proposal I have been wondering about for some time.
Many women have come to see me, some were not even 60 years of age, but many of them have been receiving the spouse's allowance. Some women have come to see me whose husbands have died, and who have been left a home but very little money, and in some cases a small mortgage. I think members on all sides of the House would agree that it is a good social point to try to encourage senior citizens to live in their homes as long as it is possible for them to do that, and as long as they prepare food and look after themselves ably, and perhaps with the help of friends and neighbours. I am sure other members have had the same difficulty with representations, trying to find alternate accommodation, and there is never enough. The difficulty, of course, is that in many instances seniors cannot afford to maintain a home. It may well be that they have a home worth $60,000 to $80,000. They may be asked to pay $1,000 in municipal taxes. Some municipalities in various provinces have given relief on the tax aspect. With the upkeep of the home and payment of taxes, senior citizens have very little money left over.
It seems to me people in that position are in similar circumstances to farmers. They have worked hard all of their lives to get rid of a mortgage so that with the equity they will have some protection for their older years. I believe the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) made the point about farmers working hard during their lives, and selling their farms. In my community the process was for them to move into town. That was a way for them to withdraw the equity that they had worked hard for, and hopefully they had money left over after the sale of the farm to live reasonably well.
People who have worked hard and have a house in an urban area have great difficulty in withdrawing equity, and in still being able to maintain their house. I have often wondered why Central Mortgage and Housing or the private mortgage sector did not look at the possibility of negative mortgages. I am suggesting to the minister that she might want to look at this in the over-all review as a next step. If a widow is living in a house with some $60,000 to $80,000 equity in it, that person could withdraw from it, say, $10,000 to $20,000 in equity. There would be no repayment schedule on that, and at the time the person either died or had to go into a nursing home for care, or for whatever reason dispose of the house,-or at some stage the estate did,-that accumulated mortgage against the property would then be due and owing.
As far as I can see this would not cost any money. It would seem to me to be just as profitable a proposition as are standard mortgages. Perhaps this could be a role for the private sector, and for Central Mortgage and Housing to guarantee that type of mortgage. To thebest of my knowledge this has never been done. It is done in terms of certain provinces and municipalities which recognize the fact that municipal taxes are onerous for senior citizens. They set the taxes aside until a person dies. This money is then collected from the sale of the property. Perhaps this would be a way to enable seniors to live in their homes many years longer than

they can afford to do now, simply because although they may have equity in their property they may not have the cash reserves or the income to maintain that house. We might allow them to withdraw some equity in the property, with no repayment schedule, and accumulate the interest payments against it. I put it forward to the ministers who are concerned about this when they next look at social assistance programs.

The other important provision in the bill before us deals with an increase in the guaranteed income supplement, which is a very important part of the old age security system in this country.
While 1 commend the minister and welcome this measure, I say to her that we have to look beyond the provision of an additional sum through the GIS and consider the plight of older people in its entirety. This is a serious question and a sad one. Indeed, I think it is a blot on the face of Canada that this country, built up by those who are now senior citizens, cannot adequately provide for those people in their old age. I say "adequately". Obviously we do make provision for them under various programs but the fact remains that many of the senior citizens of this country are living in poverty. Many were not financially prepared for retirement, some because they never saved for the future, others because their incomes were never sufficient to allow them to accumulate savings, and still others because they experienced financial tragedies during their more active years. The consequence is that many of them are forced to live below the poverty line. The fact is that 48 per cent of
October 27, 1978

the unattached people living below the poverty line are aged between 65 and 69. Those who are 70 and older represent 61.7 per cent.
There are those who say that indexation should be done away with. But in this area indexation is not, in itself, adequate, as is recognized by the bill before us increasing the amount of the GIS. Indexation is based upon the consumer price index, and I think we should examine that index to determine exactly how relevant it is to the plight of older people. I am sure the minister will agree with me that it is not an accurate or adequate measure of the position in which older people find themselves in dealing with inflation.
We feel that the consumer price index should take much greater account of components such as food, shelter and health care. I am not talking about sirloin steaks, or of food eaten outside the home. It seems to me that given the expertise which exists within Statistics Canada and within the government itself, we should be able to devise an accurate measurement of the impact of inflation upon older citizens. While there are those who might question the indexation of pensions where members of parliament or others are affected, I think there would be very few in this country who would argue against the concept of protecting senior citizens against inflation. If support of that kind is forthcoming, a heavy burden is placed upon the government to make sure that the measurement of inflation is as accurate as possible.
I submit to the minister that in present circumstances indexation based on the consumer price index is far from adequate. For example, using 1970 as a base year and $100 as the base rate, the cost of food as of September, 1978, was $211, shelter, $176.50, and health care, $168. I should like to see the consumer price index or a special price index take these factors into account. Let them deal specifically with indexation of family allowances and old age pension; in other words, the impact of inflation on low income earners in Canada. Of course, when we speak about low income earners, obviously the lowest incomes are those of older citizens who have to depend upon old age assistance as their only means of support.

They have demonstrated this attitude to those who have followed the debates over the years, as well as many people in the galleries who attend debates more than once in a while. On social issues in particular, members of the official opposition have said one
Old Age Security Act
thing in the east and another in the west. They have said one thing in Newfoundland and another in Ontario. For example, their financial critic said that they would cut public spending, yet their social policy critic urged for more public spending. Surely one must question whether there is consistency in the minds of hon. members opposite. This is the reason the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) made his speech. He brought to the attention of hon. members of the official opposition the shortcomings and gaps in their positions.
The other danger in this debate is that one could look at this bill in isolation instead of considering it as one further step along the road leading to the goal of better social security for Canadians. I suppose it is fair to look at it in isolation, but in doing so the Tories have walked into another trap, that is, looking backward rather than at the advancement and progress represented by the bill.
Yesterday and today we have seen a sequence of Tory speakers who have said that this bill does not go far enough, yet they end their speeches by saying that they support it. This bill is one of many Liberal bills passed by parliament which have established a fine foundation for social security. We have come a significant distance over the last few decades. This was emphasized by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). Canadians have told us that they support government expenditures for better pension programs. Perhaps I would not include in this group the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Construction Association or the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Workers or employees in factories engaged in assembly line work, construction, mining, heavy work or tedious factory work, tell us about their dream and hope of being given the option of retiring with a pension at an earlier age than the present one, possibly 60, as is the practice in other countries. Also, they tell us about their willingness to pay higher taxes if those increased taxes go into a pension fund designed to provide pensions at age 60 for those who want them.
The first group of people who will benefit by this kind of approach would be those who are recipients of the spouse's allowance. This group consists mostly of women who have been dependent upon their husbands most of their lives. Their dependency is real. When they lose their spouses, the widows can either apply for social assistance, which many simply do not want to do, or seek employment to support themselves, which is not easy. In many cases it results in women seeking jobs for the first time in many, many years. I am convinced the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is to be congratulated.

Reference was made in my leader's resume of the stand that we take toward the elderly about the construction of the cost of living index. I cannot remember exactly, but I am sure that the minister can tell me when there was an adjustment to the guaranteed income supplement. The government proposes in this measure, which I support, to increase that by $20 a month with respect to a single pensioner and $10 a month with respect to a married pensioner whose spouse is also a pensioner. If I knew what year the last GIS additions were made, I would be able to determine from some material which 1 obtained from the library just before I came into the chamber what the cost of living index was at that time, and I would compare it with what it is now. That is only one aspect of it, but obviously there has been a great increase in the cost of living since the guaranteed income supplement was set.
There now is an adjustment being made, a catch up for those who have been left behind, those who have no voice or pressure group to speak for them except those compassionate members of this House. I would have liked to think that more members on the government side, instead of indulging in politics, would have indulged in some compassion. Those are their spokesmen before this parliament, and those are the ones who support this bill.

The other aspect is the consumer price index which, I believe, is to be changed in the weighting which was designed on the basis of a target group devised in 1967. I believe that the November consumer price index which is to be issued on November 24 will have a different system, perhaps a different target group and a different weighting system.
The present consumer price index is improperly devised for the elderly. I would like to quote three or four elements of the 100 per cent package. Food is 24.8 per cent of that package; health and personal care 4.51 per cent; recreation, education and reading 6.89 per cent; and tobacco and alcohol 5.96 per cent. The mere enumeration of those headings and the weighting which is attributed to them is sufficient indication, I suggest, that this consumer price index is not targeted on the people about whom we are now speaking.
I have made the case in this House before, Mr. Speaker, and I will make it again, that there ought to be a special consumer price index for the elderly. The whole pattern of their purchases is different from that of people in the labour market who have an income and prospects of increasing that income from month to month and year to year. When people are backed down to a fixed income, except for measures such as this they alter that pattern. Transportation is shown as 15.18 per cent, but how many people over 70 spend 15 per cent of their expenditure package on transportation? Those who can go out are either taken out by relatives and friends or they take a bus, and that is not going to consume 15 per cent of their expenditures.
There should be an adjustment in the area of health, personal care and housing. Housing involves heating, according to my recollection of the breakdown of each of these categories. By the time people have retired they may own their house and the carrying charges thus may not be as great as for people in the work force. But the heating charge is a portion of the expenditure pattern, and for the elderly I suggest it is much higher than is attributed in the statistics.
I think improvements could be made in the statistics, and, indeed, I think Statistics Canada should devote more of its efforts to devising an appropriate form of consumer price index which could be applied to the matters under consideration today.
In the last three or four months we have heard a great deal about our falling dollar. The last quotation I had showed it below 85 cents. I have heard there is a great deal to be said for a low dollar because it is helpful to the export market. There is no question about that, of course. In fact, we are selling our patrimony cheap on contracts that have still to run out. We are selling our coal and iron in semi-refined form. It is coming back on wheels and we are paying the import price. Those who convert that coal and iron into automobiles buy it cheap and sell it back to us dear. This applies to food as well.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to take part in the debate on second reading of Bill C-5, an act to amend the Old Age Security Act. First of all I want to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) for her statement in the House. This is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that we on the government side say that more needs to be done for retired people and pensioners in Canada, especially since we feel the ravages of inflation. This legislation on old age security concerns people who receive the annual guaranteed income supplement and will qualify for a monthly increase of $20 starting on January 1. Other provisions in the legislation provide for the continued payment of the spouse's allowance for a period of six months after the death of the pensionable spouse.
Mr. Speaker, that measure by the Liberal government of Canada is welcomed by senior citizens in the electoral riding of Gaspe which I represent in the House. Most Gaspesians as well as most Canadians who receive the old age security pension and the income supplement still live in their own homes. Even though not the ideal solution to resolve every problem, this extra $20 a month for a couple will be of great help to pay school taxes, municipal rates and heating fuel.
In October, 1978, the old age security pension for an unattached person is $164.74 a month plus a supplement of $115.55, that is a total amount of $280.39. For a couple, the monthly old age security pension is $329.48 plus a guaranteed supplement of $205.22, a total allowance of $534.70 a month. In January 1979, that couple will receive an extra $20 each month, that is $554.70, while the unattached person will get $300.39.
Mr. Speaker, Canada and Sweden are the countries which have the best social programs for senior citizens. As I have said on many occasions, Canada has the best social programs in the world and Canadians are aware of the fact. For senior citizens in small municipalities with fewer than 2,500 residents the government has set up the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program-RRAP for short. Hundreds of Canadian

October 27, 1978
Old Age Security Act
couples have already taken advantage of that program and I must add, Mr. Speaker that such a program should not be abolished for a good while.
The insulation program for senior citizen housing is another example of social legislation to help needy older people. Mr. Speaker, I listened last night to the speeches of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). They could not say one thing to show that this government had passed good legislation and implemented effective programs to help older people in Canada. However, they are happy enough that the senior citizens clubs in their constituency can benefit from the New Horizons program and that this government assists in building meeting and recreation facilities for senior citizens through the Canada Works program. Those are revolutionary programs and it is unfortunate that the opposition cannot recognize it occasionally. However, I applaud the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who said the following in his speech yesterday:

I have to say that to me it was a delight to sit here this afternoon and hear the minister speak with pride about our pension legislation, to make it clear that it is here to stay, that things like indexing have to continue and that we have to continue to make other improvements for our older people.

be able to say that the federal government should get involved in that field of responsibility? I congratulate her for that. I congratulate her as well for bringing the matter forward because, as has been indicated by other speakers in this debate, the principles in this bill are supported by the official opposition.
I will not speak very long, Mr. Speaker, because it is the intention of the official opposition to allow this bill to proceed through second reading and to the committee where its background can be examined. But I want to say at the outset that we support the bill, the effect of which is to increase the amount of the guaranteed income supplement by $20 for a single pensioner and $10 for a married pensioner whose spouse is also a pensioner, and to extend the spouse's allowance for six months after the death of the pensionable spouse. That principle is supportable, if not on moral grounds, which I think it is, then on statistical grounds.
Statistics relating to senior citizens in Canada are rather alarming as a result of inflation which has come about by reason of the policies of this government. Inflation is an extremely serious thing for senior citizens. Dealing with the value of the dollar in 1968 in terms of food for senior citizens, that dollar is only worth 43.4 cents; in terms of housing, it is worth today only 48.7 cents; in respect of clothing, it is worth 64.1 cents; in respect of transportation, it is worth only 53.7 cents; in terms of health and personal care, it is worth 53 cents; in terms of recreation and reading, it is worth 58.2 cents.

October 27, 1978

As Canadians generally have suffered from inflation, 1 think the impact of that phenomenon on our society-for which the government must take considerable blame-rests heavily on the shoulders, on the pocketbooks and on the peace of mind of our senior citizens. So when the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), a few moments ago in this debate, asked where the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton stood, let me say to him, through you, sir, that the member for Grenville-Carleton supports this bill. Like the members of his party, he believes that the job of the government is to help the disadvantaged to the extent that society can reasonably help the disadvantaged, just as it is the job of government in a society like ours to create an atmosphere where those who are not so disadvantaged can use their initiative and their entrepreneurial skills and take the risks to help build this country.
The question was asked of me where we stand. I put it to the hon. member that that is where we stand and, in terms of the senior citizens in this country, our party does not take second place to any other party in terms of its support of their betterment and their welfare.
But there is one thing that the hon. member for Davenport said which rather disturbed me. He said that it was his party which brought in the hospitalization scheme for Canadians, that his party proposed a hospitalization scheme in 1957, just before they were defeated. Let me point out that there was a little catch to it, and that is that the scheme had to be approved by the provinces having the majority of the population in the country.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) called it for what it was, a fraud and a swindle, and pledged that if the Conservative government was put in office in 1957 those conditions would be removed, which they were. So the hospitalization scheme that we have today in this country has as its basis that which was proposed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert when he beat the Liberal government in 1957.
I think one problem that arose-I do not want to fall into that trap-is that this debate has not followed the example given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. A little trading game has been played, a little political game on the backs of the senior citizens. But I will say to the hon. member for Davenport that he is wrong in what he said. 1 felt I had to rise to correct his statement.
Quite frankly, I wish we would follow the request made by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and extend the spouse's allowance all the way, as had been advocated before. I assume from what the minister said that if the country could afford it, it could be done. What she said to me is that she has consulted with her colleagues but because of the restraint program which is in effect, it cannot be done.
I do not think there is any person in the House of Commons who would not want to see this program extended if it could be, and 1 assume that that kind of investigation was made and the extension of that program was turned down. I would be terribly shocked if it were turned down in order to be advanced perhaps next spring, just in advance of a general election. 1
Old Age Security Act
think that would be the height of hypocrisy and I live in the hope that we will not play that kind of action game with senior citizens or any other group in Canada. I think we have to be honest about that.
I rise for a second reason and that is with respect to a remark made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) about the equalization payments and the attitude of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield). As I heard the hon. member for Gloucester, he was saying that the hon. member for Halifax, the former leader of this party and former premier of Nova Scotia, took a stand the other day against equalization payments when he asked a question in the House. I heard that question from my sick bed at home and I heard the answer, and I must say that if that was the conclusion reached by the hon. member for Gloucester, then he needs his hearing fixed. I would commend to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that she invite the hon. member for Gloucester to go down to her department and have his ears examined, if not his head, with respect to that position.
I feel I have to say this because I come from central Canada. It is very easy for members from eastern Canada, from New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, to support the concept of equalization payments, but it is sometimes hard in Ontario to support that concept. However, I support it and I am somewhat concerned when I hear that kind of misconstruction placed on the question put by the hon. member for Halifax by the hon. member for Gloucester.
I have no problem supporting the equalization principle, nor does the federal Conservative party, nor does the Conservative party in the province of Ontario. This has always been the case. That is the reason we are here as a nation. The concept of equalization is so important to us in Canada that our party has taken the view, against the advice of some constitutional tinkerers, that we should have that principle enshrined in the constitution of our country. I say that knowing that there are some on the other side of the House who would like to say that as the mother and father of every social program in Canada they are also the mother and father of the equalization system in this country. Well, they are not. It is axiomatic that it is necessary in terms of our confederation, and it is supported generally.
The hon. member for St. John's East referred to the Kingston document which was the result of a meeting of all the then premiers of Canada who happened to be Progressive Conservatives. That number has been augmented to such a degree by the bringing in of Mr. Buchanan of Nova Scotia and Mr. Lyon of Manitoba-we almost had Angus MacLean by one seat in Prince Edward Island-and Mr. Hatfield has been returned, that the next meeting of premiers will almost be a meeting of Convervatives; we wait only one event, and that is the installation of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) as the Prime Minister of Canada. That is coming. Our system needs flush-

ing out now and again and can certainly stand a flushing out now.
Our approach to federal-provincial relations goes far beyond equalization. There is the whole question of tariffs and transportation policy, a host of areas which have been left relatively unexplored, except as to user-pay, in terms of the welfare of the whole country. I thought I would make those things clear.
The hon. member for Gloucester also mentioned that it had been the policy of our party to allocate too many resources to help the poor people. 1 listened to him say that this morning. The Progressive Conservative party has never taken that position. What it has said is that we must begin paying more than lip service to developing a larger economic pie, because if we fail to do so we shall experience great difficulty in supporting economic programs to help the disadvantaged. It is in that area the emphasis must lie over the next few years.
This does involve the cutting back of government. It does involve giving up some programs which I for one, as a member of parliament, would dearly like to see. I represent the people in the national capital area. One of the issues in this House has been the question of grants in lieu of taxes. The mayor of Ottawa has said it is worth $150 a household because the government is not carrying its weight with respect to grants in lieu of taxes in the city. I would love to have the luxury of being able to say that the government can give that $150 a household, but I cannot honestly support that now, much as I support the principle. What is worse, the reason I cannot advocate it is not because something has happened in the world. It is not because there has been a change somewhere in the country-ours is still a rich country with large resources. It is that something that has happened to the government which has wasted those resources and opportunities over ten years so that this inequity cannot be rectified.
When the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) asks the government whether it will accede to changing the grants in lieu of taxes this year and rectifying the situation, the hon. member is engaging in window dressing because he knows that the policies of the party he has supported since he has been here have brought about an economic situation which makes it impossible for him to get his wish and impossible for me to get mine. It also makes it impossible for a lot of members of the House to have a great many of the programs they dearly want for their constituents.
That is the tragedy of the last ten years. It is not restraint, it is what led up to it. The attitude of government in the last ten years has been that we had a bottomless pit, that they could dig into it and continue to dig into it and there was no tomorrow. They did this in spite of warnings from the Economic Council and its predecessor, from every responsible organization in Canada, that there was a bottom to the pit and that the government's spending habit had to stop. Now we find ourselves in a position where, indeed, it has to stop.

speechtext: What about the four billion in mortgage payments?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: The hon. member mentions the mortgage payments. Somehow or other we must begin to create an atmosphere of incentive in order that we can build again. Mr. Speaker, this government spills almost as much as it spends. The hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) mentioned the mortgage program. He says to us that it is too rich for Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: Four billion dollars.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: He dearly wishes he had brought in the mortgage program and the property tax deduction proposal himself because it is an imaginative program. But that is not the important thing about his intervention. It is this. While the government were saying that Canadians were too rich to deserve a tax break, that the home owners, 60 per cent of whom make less than $18,000, were the filthy rich and could not be helped, they were entering into and defending a deal for four office complexes in the Ottawa region under lease-back arrangements, the results of which were going to cost the government $179 million more than would have been the case had they gone the more conventional route. And this is not an assertion by me, it is an assertion by a Senate committee, headed by Liberals including Liberal Senator Everett and Senator Giguere, a committee which condemned the government for its flagrant squandering of public money, money which might be used to help constituents in Laprairie.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: That's the pity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext: As my hon. friend says, that's the pity. We have come to the point at which one of the central institutions for the public good in Canada, CMHC, is being examined by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and rumors are that charges will be laid. That is maladministration. That is waste. That is some kind of wrongheadedness. But that is what we have come to. We have come to the position at which, with respect to Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) at the opening defended the indefensible and said it was an excellent transaction for the government. Robert Campeau stood on his hind legs and grinned into the television cameras and said this was a good deal for Campeau and a good deal for the federal government. He was only half right.

speechtext: What about the bill?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE GUARANTEED INCOME SUPPLEMENT
speechtext:
I will tell hon. members how this relates to the bill. There is not another member of parliament who would wish more than I that the $179 million which was wasted on Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere, the money spent on things which are going to be found out in the investigation of York Place, the glass monstrosity of the Bank of Canada which will cost us millions and which is a monument to the architect rather than to good sense, and the $210 million blown on the unemployment insurance program, could go to the objectives spoken about so eloquently by the Minister
October 27, 1978

of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) when I heard her speak yesterday.
That is the tragedy of all this. We speak of what we have done about redistributing income in Canada. From 1968 to 1978 the budget in Canada has grown from $10 billion to almost $50 billion, and yet the proportion of Canadian families below the poverty line is just about the same as it was in 1968. We have not succeeded in redistributing income successfully at all. Perhaps it is because we have concentrated so much on redistribution and not on developing the economic pie upon which redistribution could be based and on which a change in it could be based.
That is why I feel sorry about the situation our country is in today. I do not pretend to be any more compassionate than any other member of this House, nor do I take second place to any other member. But I wonder when the day is going to come when we are going to be asked to support proper social programs, and when we will have a government which has a real commitment to restraint and to priorizing in terms of where our country is going, so that we will not waste as we have, so that we will not dissipate the riches we have, so that we can give our children and our children's children some opportunities, so that we can do something about unemployment which now stands so high and so that we can do something for senior citizens who, when they speak to me about the benefits of this bill, as good as they are, say, "Mr. Baker, that still does not get me out of the problem in which I find myself'. They tell me that they are worried about their future and still feel insecure.
We support this bill. The minister tried to say that I was insecure about my future. That is not in my hands. I am talking about the senior citizens who have spoken to me. They still say that, as commendable as these steps are-I commend the minister for taking these steps, and this party intends to support the bill and allow it to go to committee today-the government ought not to break its arm patting itself on the back. It has our support with respect to every worth while program. It has the support of all sides of the House. We just wish that in terms of the management of the business of the country the government would give us an equal dose of common sense. The Canadian people are sick and tired of waste and of seeing large tax increases month after month and then finding themselves further and further behind. When we put this bill through today, perhaps the government will bend its efforts to get to the root of many other problems. We will support appropriate social programs in Canada.
